core_principles.text: Engage the glutes, squeeze the quads, and draw the ribs down toward the pelvis before starting to maintain a neutral spine and proper pelvic alignment.
If unable to maintain a straight body line, modify the movement by dropping to the knees while keeping the hips aligned with the shoulders and the core tight.
Perform a full range of motion by lowering until the chest nearly touches the floor, ensuring the chest leads the way down rather than the belly or chin.
If strength is the limiting factor, elevate hands on a box or bench to practice the full range of motion without compromising technique.
Aim for a 45-degree angle between the torso and elbows, forming an arrow shape with the arms during the descent.
Retract the shoulder blades slightly and keep them down and back throughout the movement.

common_mistakes.text: Lifting the hips into the air during the lowering phase due to an anterior pelvic tilt and core disengagement.
Allowing the hips to sag toward the floor due to an inactive or fatigued core.
Performing partial reps by only bending the elbows slightly and stopping far above the ground.
Flaring the elbows out excessively into a T-shape away from the body.
Tucking the elbows too tightly against the ribs during the push-up.
Allowing the shoulders to creep up toward the ears or drop before the hips due to insufficient scapular control.

consequences.text: Lifting the hips into an anterior pelvic tilt breaks the straight line of the body and results in a lack of abdominal engagement.
Allowing the hips to sag puts undue pressure on the lower back and reduces overall exercise effectiveness.
Stopping far above the ground in a partial push-up prevents the chest muscles from working to their full potential.
Flaring the elbows into a T-shape places unnecessary stress on the shoulders and increases the risk of injury.
Tucking the elbows too tightly against the ribs reduces chest muscle engagement and shifts the load primarily to the triceps.
Lacking scapular control during the push-up places the neck and upper trapezius muscles into overdrive.
